power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Protocols (treatment manuals) in Music Therapy: an international survey
table.existing_data_explanation: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions:
The following questions are asked: 
Q1: Which variables can be identified that potentially influence the use of protocols within music therapy? 
Q2: What is the most common motivation behind protocol use or deviation from this for the therapist? 
Q3: From the therapist's perspective, does protocol use influence the client's therapy attendance and approach?

The main hypotheses to be tested are: 
H1: The use of protocols is expected to vary depending on the preferred therapeutic approach, years of experience, clinical setting, age, familiarity with, and attitude towards treatment manuals. 
H2: The attitude that treatment manuals interfere with the creative and spontaneous nature of musical interaction is expected to be most commonly identified by therapists as a reason to deviate from them
H3: Treatment manuals are expected to be perceived as contrasting with the personalised approach based on the clients' needs, this is thought to reduce motivation for the client.
table.design_dependent_variables: Therapists' attitudes towards treatment manuals are rated using sliders (1-100 visual analog sliders with indications of scale, i.e., 'not at all' to 'very much' etc) and include questions like: proportion of time they are used/ not used, reasons for use or deviation from protocols, level of importance and reasons for this, how their usage motivates/demotivates both therapist and client.
table.study_design_overview: There are no conditions as it is an observational questionnaire study.
table.statistical_tests:
To test all three hypotheses, we will perform a crosstabulation analysis, also known as contingency table analysis, comparing 
1) variables such as age, years of independent practice, therapeutic approach, country, client group, therapy goals AND use of protocols 
2) reasons to deviate from the use of protocols AND therapy goals, motivation (therapist), therapeutic approach, 
3) motivation (client) AND use of protocol, (significance) personalised approach. 
Within crosstabs a x2 (chi-square) statistic test will be applied between cells, to ascertain the statistical significance (p < .05) of a particular variable, e.g. therapy goals, motivation (therapist) or motivation (client).
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Outliers will not be defined - all values will be included. Exclusions will be based on the following exclusion criteria: no qualified practitioners, respondents who didn't complete 80% of the questions, or if a respondent took extremely long to complete the questionnaire (more than 1 week since starting the questionnaire).
table.sample_size: We will offer the survey for roughly 3 months with a minimum sample goal of 60, but stopping recruitment at 200 participants.
table.additional_comments:
Data collection is almost finalised but not yet inspected.

Secondary analyses that address the first research question will use multiple linear regression to predict ratings of protocol use and ratings of attitudes towards protocols from the factors named under analysis 1)

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p > .05", "p=.43", "p=.65"), Sentence = c("No other settings showed significant associations (p > .05).", "Neither association was statistically significant: perceived negative effects on therapist motivation, p=.43; perceived negative effects on client motivation, p=.65.", "Neither association was statistically significant: perceived negative effects on therapist motivation, p=.43; perceived negative effects on client motivation, p=.65." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Treatment manuals and protocols (TM/Ps) are increasingly used to standardise clinical music therapy interventions, yet they often neglect clients' motivational needs, which are essential for engagement and recovery.
Therapists may adapt or deviate from established TM/Ps to accommodate individual preferences or motivational factors.
This study examined music therapists' attitudes, practices, and reasons for deviation regarding TM/P use across diverse clinical settings.

Method Qualified music therapists (N=93) from 23 countries completed an online survey, available in five languages, capturing demographic data, theoretical orientation, views on TM/Ps, and reasons for deviation.
Descriptive statistics summarised the sample, while crosstabulations with χ² tests and ordinal logistic regression were used to examine relationships among variables.
Therapists held mixed views on TM/Ps, acknowledging their benefits for structure while expressing concerns about diminished personalisation, spontaneity, and motivation.
Although many perceived rigid protocols as detrimental to engagement, these attitudes did not significantly predict TM/P usage.
Usage varied by context (lower in educational settings) and theoretical approach (lower in anthroposophic and attachment-oriented, higher in integrative frameworks).
Beliefs about TM/P importance, rather than experience or age, appeared as stronger determinants of use.

While exploratory and statistically modest, the findings highlight persistent tensions between standardisation and individualisation in music therapy, and that these concerns are shared by many practitioners.
The results suggest a need for TM/Ps that support flexible client-centred practice, while retaining sufficient structure for clinical and research purposes.
In clinical sciences, treatment manuals and protocols (TM/Ps) have been reported to be one of the most common ways interventions are disseminated to practising clinicians (Becker et al., 2013).

text.text: Protocolised clinical work can offer various advantages, such as establishing standardised interventions, facilitating training for less experienced practitioners, and enabling the collection of empirical data for evidence-based practice (Morrison, 2017).
text.formatted: Protocolised clinical work can offer various advantages, such as establishing standardised interventions, facilitating training for less experienced practitioners, and enabling the collection of empirical data for evidence-based practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Morrison, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, despite these potential advantages, the adoption and perceived value of TM/Ps in practice can vary significantly across disciplines.

Since their inception, treatment manuals have been surrounded by controversy, particularly in fields like psychotherapy and the creative arts therapies, where individualised, relational, and improvisational elements are central to the therapeutic process (Carroll & Nuro, 2002).

text.text: In music therapy, these challenges are especially pronounced, as they arise not only from its highly individualised nature and reliance on a therapeutic relationship, but also from the significant difficulty of protocolising the musical aspect, which, in general terms, serves a similar function to words in verbal psychotherapy (Bunt & Stige, 2014).

text.text: The present study is informed by the authors' positioning as neuroscience-informed music therapists and/or researchers.

In this context, neuroscience-informed music therapy refers to the integration of relevant knowledge about neural, cognitive, sensorimotor, affective, developmental, and social processes into the understanding, selection, adaptation, and evaluation of music therapy interventions.

This perspective recognises that music therapy is a relational and context-sensitive practice and cannot be attributed to neurobiological processes alone (De L' Etoile & LaGasse, 2013; Moore & LaGasse, 2018; Magee & Stewart, 2015).
text.formatted: This perspective recognises that music therapy is a relational and context-sensitive practice and cannot be attributed to neurobiological processes alone <ref type="bibr">(De L' Etoile & LaGasse, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Moore & LaGasse, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Magee & Stewart, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: It also includes neurological approaches to music therapy and rehabilitation, including Neurologic Music Therapy® (Thaut & Hömberg, 2025).
text.formatted: It also includes neurological approaches to music therapy and rehabilitation, including Neurologic Music Therapy® <ref type="bibr">(Thaut & Hömberg, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The lead author's clinical practice is additionally informed by psychotherapeutic principles, in which the therapeutic relationship-grounded in empathy, attunement, and collaboration-is regarded as a central vehicle for therapeutic change.

These perspectives inform how we understand music therapy: music is not only an active therapeutic medium, but its therapeutic potential emerges through the relationship and interaction between therapist and client.
It is precisely this particular musical aspect that characterises music therapy due to its deeply interactive nature.

A core aspect of music therapy is the intersubjective musical interaction, in which music therapists shape and respond to clients' expressions to foster attunement and shared meaning, processes that directly support client motivation and engagement (Ansdell & Pavlicevic, 2004; Bruscia, 2014).

text.text: Drawing on developmental psychology, musical mirroring and attunement in early pre-verbal communication provide a foundation for using music to build therapeutic relationships (Malloch and Trevarthen, 2009).

text.text: Co-creation and improvisation further emphasise how meaning emerges from shared musical narratives, allowing for non-verbal expression and agency (Mossler et al., 2022).

text.text: This interactive and often spontaneous nature distinguishes music therapy from (music-based) protocols used by other disciplines, in which musical play and spontaneity are not features of the intervention.
At the same time, the demand for research rigour requires replicable methods and therapeutic consistency (Rolvsjord et al., 2005).
text.formatted: At the same time, the demand for research rigour requires replicable methods and therapeutic consistency <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Rolvsjord et al., 2005)</ref>.

This can create tension, as music therapy is both a highly idiosyncratic, personalised intervention and a discipline that must be understandable and evaluable by non-music therapists, e.g., researchers, stakeholders, policy makers, and other health professionals (Magee & Stewart, 2015).

text.text: Despite this tension, TM/Ps have been developed across music therapy approaches and clinical settings.

Examples include structured descriptions of improvisational music therapy for autism research (Geretsegger et al., 2012; Bieleninik et al., 2017), Guided Imagery and Music (Grocke, 2010) and music therapy methods for cognitive rehabilitation (Baker and Tamplin, 2006).

text.text: In neurorehabilitation, protocolised music-based interventions have also been developed for speech-language, motor, and gait-related goals, including Melodic Intonation Therapy and Speech and Music Therapy for Aphasia, Music-supported therapy and Rhythmic Auditory Stimulation (Hurkmans et al., 2015; Sparks & Holland, 1976; Thaut & Hoemberg, 2025; Thaut & Abiru, 2010).

text.text: Although these examples demonstrate that TM/Ps can be developed for a range of clinical aims, relatively little is known about how such resources are perceived, used, or adapted by practising music therapists.

It remains unclear whether and to what extent TM/Ps are experienced as beneficial aids or conversely as restrictive constraints, and how their use aligns with the lived realities and clinical philosophies of music therapists working in diverse contexts.

In particular, empirical knowledge remains limited on how music therapists balance the demands of standardisation with their need for clinical flexibility, and how they navigate decisions to adhere to, adapt, or deviate from TM/Ps in everyday practice.
Motivation appears to be a key concept in this balancing act.
When clients (or even therapists) are unmotivated, strict adherence to TM/Ps may have counterproductive effects on engagement and outcomes.

Yet, client motivation has been comparatively under emphasised in the design and reporting of music-based protocols, despite its centrality to therapy engagement (Dimitriadis et al., 2024a; Verrienti et al., 2023).

text.text: Recent work in music therapy and neurorehabilitation suggests that motivating elements, such as musical reward, patient preference, and active involvement, can be integrated into structured interventions to improve adherence and effectiveness, particularly in populations such as stroke survivors (Dimitriadis et al., 2024b; Thomson et al., 2022).

text.text: However, little is known about how music therapists decide whether to adhere to, adapt, or deviate from TM/Ps when client needs, engagement, or clinical circumstances change during practice.

These decisions may be closely related to the motivation of both clients and therapists and raise important questions about the gap between the standardisation promoted by TM/Ps and the realities of sustaining motivation and engagement in clinical practice.

To examine associations between TM/P use and therapist-and practice-related characteristics.
We addressed the following hypotheses:

H1: Frequency of TM/P use would be associated with therapist age, years of independent practice, therapeutic orientation, and clinical setting H2: Amongst therapists reporting TM/P use, more frequent deviation from TM/Ps would be associated with stronger agreement that TM/Ps restrict spontaneity and play H3: Stronger agreement that TM/Ps may negatively affect client and therapist motivation would be associated with less frequent TM/P use.
Associations between TM/P use or deviation frequency and other attitudes towards TM/Ps were examined exploratorily.
Participants were qualified music therapists who could complete the survey in English, Dutch, Greek, Spanish, or German.

The survey was made available in these languages to reduce language barriers, evaluate potential regional differences, and increase access for music therapists across different countries and professional communities.

English was included as a widely used language for international academic and professional communication, while Dutch, Greek, Spanish, and German translations were provided to enable participation in the languages represented by the professional networks and associations through which the survey was distributed.

Recruitment was conducted through two primary avenues: (1) posts shared on relevant LinkedIn groups for music therapists, and (2) announcements and embedded survey links distributed via email newsletters of professional music therapy organisations, including the British, Dutch, Greek, Spanish and German associations for music therapy.
Inclusion criteria required participants to be qualified music therapists actively engaged in clinical practice, on a career break, or retired.

Exclusion criteria were: lack of recognised professional music therapy qualification or registration, incomplete survey responses (less than 60% of questions answered), or survey time exceeding one week from initiation.
The 60% completion threshold was selected a priori as a pragmatic criterion to retain responses containing sufficient information to address at least one of the study hypotheses.

Demographic information collected included age, gender, years of independent practice (used as an indicator of years of clinical experience), preferred therapeutic approach, clinical setting, country, and primary client group.

Survey questions addressing the hypotheses were developed by the authors on the basis of clinical experience, current music therapy practice, and literature on TM/Ps, protocol use, and motivation in music-based interventions.
The initial item pool was discussed within a committee of experienced music therapists and researchers, who evaluated content relevance, clarity, and coverage of the study aims.
The survey was then reviewed by practising music therapists in each of the five languages to assess face validity and clinical relevance.
The survey was first drafted in English and then translated into Dutch, Greek, Spanish and German by bilingual music therapists or researchers.
Translations were checked by native-speaking music therapists to support conceptual and linguistic equivalence with the English version.
As the questionnaire was newly developed and not a standardised or previously validated instrument, formal psychometric validation and back-translation were not undertaken.
Discrepancies or ambiguities identified during language review were discussed and resolved by consensus.
The resulting 53-item online survey was administered using Qualtrics (Qualtrics, Provo, UT).
The survey was open from 17 December 2024 tο 28 February 2025 and was designed to take 15 minutes to complete (Md = 13.36 minutes, range 4.38 minutes -87.3 hours).

It included multiple-choice and slider-based items addressing TM/P use, frequency of use and motivation, reasons for deviation and non-use, therapist motivation and attitudes towards TM/Ps, demographic characteristics, therapeutic orientation, clinical setting and client group.
Several closed-ended items included an optional "other" free-text field, allowing respondents to indicate reasons, attitudes, or response options not represented by the predefined categories.
These responses were reviewed descriptively to identify potentially omitted perspectives; they were not subjected to formal qualitative analysis.
The full questionnaire and response options are provided in Supplementary Material S1.
Respondents rated agreement with statements about positive and negative attitudes towards TM/Ps using visual analogue slider scales ranging from 0 ('strongly disagree') to 100 ('strongly agree').

The items addressed perceived benefits, such as structure, treatment effectiveness, replicability, and communication with other professionals, as well as concerns about rigidity, reduced flexibility, spontaneity, individualisation, and motivation.
Positive and negatively worded items were included to capture contrasting views of TM/Ps and to reduce acquiescence bias.
When first accessing the online survey, respondents received information about the study's purpose, procedures, voluntary nature, and data confidentiality.
Informed consent was obtained electronically before they proceeded to the survey.
On completion, participants were shown an automated debriefing page that thanked them for their participation,

text.text: Prior to statistical analysis, the dataset was screened for missing, implausible, or potentially erroneous values.
For continuous variables, values more than three standard deviations from the mean and boxplots were examined for potential outliers.
For categorical variables, frequency distributions were examined for impossible or clearly miscoded categories.
No observations were removed solely on the basis of an outlier value.

To address the study's aims and test the main hypotheses, descriptive statistics were calculated to explore current usage of TM/Ps, and crosstabulation analyses were performed using SPSS Statistics Version 29.0.2 (IBM, Armonk, NY) to provide insights into the associations between the hypothesised variables.

More specifically, Chi-square tests of independence were used because the attitude and opinion items were recoded from 1-100 slider ratings into ordinal response categories (e.g., strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree, strongly agree), and were analysed alongside categorical therapist and practice variables.
This approach enabled us to examine whether the distribution of TM/P attitudes and use differed across therapist and professional-context categories.
H1 was tested using crosstabulation between TM/P use and therapist age, years of clinical practice (as an index of independent experience), and client group (age and setting).
Associations between therapeutic orientation and frequency of TM/P use were examined using ordinal logistic regression, as most therapists indicated multiple options.
Frequency of TM/P use was treated as an ordered categorical outcome with five response categories: never, rarely, about half the time, usually, and always.
Ordinal logistic regression was selected because TM/P use frequency was ordinal rather than continuous and participants could select more than one therapeutic orientation.
Each therapeutic orientation was entered as a binary predictor variable (selected vs. not selected).

In addition to the hypothesis-driven analyses on practice-related factors, exploratory chi-square analyses examined associations between frequency of TM/P use and recoded (see below) attitude ratings towards TM/Ps.

H2 was tested by first describing the frequency of TM/P deviation and the reported reasons for deviation, followed by crosstabulation between frequency of deviation and agreement with 10 attitude statements, including the hypothesised statement that 'TM/Ps are restrictive, as they interfere with spontaneity and play'.
Finally, H3 was tested using descriptive statistics for two items concerning motivation, as well as crosstabulation between agreement with these items and frequency of TM/P use.

Agreement ratings were originally collected using slider scales from 0 to 100.
For crosstabulation analyses, these continuous scores were re-coded into a 5-point ordinal scale (strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree, strongly agree).
Specifically, values 0-20 were coded as 'strongly disagree', 21-40 as 'disagree', 41-60 as 'neutral', 61-80 as 'agree ', and 81-100 as 'strongly agree'.
This holds for all analyses with the exception of the multiple linear regression, which used continuous ratings.
Statistical tests were evaluated using a two-sided significance threshold of α = .05.
A total of 101 survey responses were received.
Eight responses were excluded because they did not meet the inclusion criteria.
Therefore, 93 responses (22 male, 69 female, 2 self-specify/prefer not to say) were included in the analysis.
Participants' ages ranged from 22 to 68 years, and years of independent practice ranged from 0 to 33 years (M=9.21, SD=9.01).
Categorical responses were viewed for completeness and plausibility; no impossible or clearly miscoded categories were identified.

One participant recorded a survey completion time of 87.3 hours, substantially longer than the overall completion time distribution; however, as the participant's item-response pattern was otherwise plausible, the response was retained.
The median survey time was 13.36 minutes (range= 4.38 minutes to 87.3 hours).
The sample represented a diverse group of music therapists, spanning a broad range of years of independent experience, with most (approximately 42 %) holding at least a master's degree.
Theoretical orientations varied, with neurologic/neuroscience-informed, humanistic, and music-centred frameworks being the most common.
With regards to survey language, the predominant responses were in Dutch (43%) and English (35%), followed by German (9.7%), Greek (7.5%), and Spanish (5.4%).
See Supplementary Material S2 for more detailed information on demographic characteristics.

Participants reported working with a range of client age groups, with adults (>18 years) being the most common (73.3%), although half of the respondents (50.5%) currently work or had worked (also) with children, as multiple answers were possible.

text.text: Overall, 72.1% stated deviating from TM/Ps about half the time or more.

Regarding the reasons to deviate from TM/Ps, the highest mean rating was observed for "When clients are losing interest" (M = 69.3%, SD = 23.6), followed by "When clients' functional limitations require it" (M = 68.4%, SD = 23.7), "When the client wishes to stop" (M = 66.5%, SD = 23.6), and "When I see an alternative option for addressing clients' needs during the session" (M = 60.5%, SD = 26.4).
In addition, 45% of the respondents selected the ''other'' category.
Their responses included perceived counterproductive effects, client preferences, spontaneous events during the session, and research-related constraints.
Exploratory, non-preregistered chi-square analyses were performed to examine associations between frequency of deviation and agreement with ten attitude statements about TM/Ps.
Table 2 presents the results of these analyses.

text.text: Significant associations were observed for attitudes concerning the importance of TM/P for practice, professional communication, therapy accessibility and restrictions on spontaneity and play.

Across these four associations, inspection of the crosstabbed variables indicated that stronger agreement with the statements was associated with more frequent protocol deviation (see further Table 2).

text.text: The present study set out to clarify how music therapists view and use TM/Ps, particularly regarding deviation from these TM/Ps and their perceived impact on motivation in clinical practice.

An international sample of music therapists was surveyed, and crosstabulation and regression analyses were conducted to examine how attitudes, therapeutic frameworks, experience, and demographic variables relate to TM/P use and perception.
The findings suggest that protocol use may be shaped by therapists' theoretical orientations, work context, and attitudes, rather than by age or length of clinical experience.
The first hypothesis proposed that protocol use would vary according to therapist approach, experience, setting, age, and attitudes.
This was only partially supported.
Contrary to expectations, neither work experience nor age significantly predicted TM/P use, suggesting that TM/P adoption is not simply a matter of career stage or generational cohort.

One possible explanation is that awareness of TM/Ps has grown across the profession, so both newer and more experienced therapists are exposed to TM/Ps and use them when they fit their work setting and training background.
Clinical setting emerged as a significant negative predictor of TM/P use, but only for educational environments.
A relatively high proportion of therapists working in educational settings reported less frequent TM/P use despite the structured nature of these contexts.

This apparent paradox may be explained by institutional demands, such as the Individual Education Plan (IEP), which, especially in countries like the UK or the USA, may supplant all other protocols, even clinical ones.
Music therapists in schools are indeed often required to work within a hybrid role that blends therapy with education and consultation (Robertson, 2000).
text.formatted: Music therapists in schools are indeed often required to work within a hybrid role that blends therapy with education and consultation <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Robertson, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Regression analyses indicated that respondents' theoretical approach predicted TM/P use in some cases.

Specifically, therapists endorsing anthroposophic and attachment-oriented approaches reported less frequent TM/P use, whereas those identifying with an integrative approach reported more frequent use.
One interpretation is that anthroposophic music therapy relies on individualised, holistic care and favours 'diagnostic flexibility' over standardised procedures (Intveen & Edwards, 2013).
text.formatted: One interpretation is that anthroposophic music therapy relies on individualised, holistic care and favours 'diagnostic flexibility' over standardised procedures <ref type="bibr">(Intveen & Edwards, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, attachment-oriented therapists may prioritise the need for adaptive, relationship-based work with clients whose insecure attachments require flexibility and relational attunement (Slade, 2019).

structured techniques from multiple models, including manualised interventions, when these are perceived as fitting the client's needs (Jones-Smith, 2019).
However, the unequal dispersion over theoretical approaches means that these results should be interpreted cautiously.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, therapists' attitudes towards TM/Ps themselves were most strongly related to self-reported frequency of use.

Three specific attitudes, namely TM/Ps' perceived importance for practice, contribution to therapists' confidence, and concerns about ΤΜ/Ps hindering personalised approaches, were all significantly associated with increased usage frequency.
Therapists who felt that TM/Ps impede their ability to personalise care reported less use in practice, whereas those who did not share this concern reported more regular protocol use.
As might be expected, a clear majority who strongly agreed that TM/Ps are important for practice reported 'always' using them.
In contrast, none of those who disagreed that TM/Ps are important reported 'always' using them.
Heightened concerns over TM/Ps as barriers to individualised care were associated with decreased use, with most of those expressing this concern reporting infrequent TM/P use.

Spontaneity and creativity also emerged as salient factors: therapists viewing TM/Ps as restrictive in these areas were considerably less likely to adopt them, underscoring the discipline's commitment to musical/clinical improvisation and creativity.
This highlights the need for protocols designed to carefully balance structure with creative flexibility to gain therapist acceptance.
Importantly but also unsurprisingly, therapists indicated that protocol use should never take precedence over client needs.
Across items, therapists consistently prioritised individualised care and clinical judgement, also amongst those with generally positive views of standardisation.
Many also reported that, in their experience, adherence to TM/Ps does not on its own determine clinical outcomes.

Rather than being viewed as directives to be followed rigidly, TM/Ps may offer a shared reference point for treatment planning, documenting intervention components, and communicating about treatment with other professionals when they are adapted to the client and clinical context.

The observed associations between positive attitudes towards TM/Ps-for example, perceiving them as important for practice or confidence-enhancing-and more frequent TM/P use are consistent with this interpretation.
Regarding the second hypothesis, which focused on reasons for deviation from TM/Ps, the findings provide partial support for the proposed role of perceived restrictions on spontaneity and play.
In the exploratory analyses, agreement that TM/Ps restrict spontaneity and play was associated with more frequent self-reported deviation.
However, this was not the only attitude associated with deviation frequency.

Positive associations were also observed for attitudes concerning the importance of TM/Ps for practice, the contribution to professional communication, and their perceived influence on therapy accessibility.

More broadly, the most highly agreed with reasons for deviating (loss of interest, functional limitations, a client's wish to stop, and the emergence of alternative therapeutic options) suggest that deviation may often occur in response to immediate clinical circumstances and perceived clinical needs.
Together, these results portray deviation not as a simple rejection of P r e p r i n t

text.text: The third hypothesis proposed that TM/Ps might conflict with personalised approaches, potentially dampening motivation for both clients and therapists.

This notion was supported at the level of reported attitudes (many therapists believed that TM/Ps that do not sufficiently reflect client goals can negatively affect motivation), but these concerns did not translate into clear differences in reported TM/P use.
This discrepancy suggests that motivational reservations alone may not be enough to drive non-use or rejection of TM/Ps.

It is possible that therapists weigh perceived structural or pragmatic benefits (e.g., clarity, documentation, interdisciplinary communication) against motivational concerns and choose to use TM/Ps while adapting them in practice.

In this study, we focused primarily on music therapists' perceptions of how TM/Ps may affect the maintenance of client motivation and engagement, and secondarily on therapists' own motivation to use TM/Ps.
Future research could examine more explicitly whether and how motivational processes mediate associations between protocol characteristics and therapeutic outcomes.
Overall, our findings suggest that TM/Ps occupy an ambivalent but potentially productive position in music therapy practice.
On one hand, many therapists in this sample associate TM/Ps with inflexibility and procedural burden, and a substantial proportion report using them rarely.
On the other hand, respondents also recognise important advantages, particularly for research, communication with stakeholders, and providing a degree of structural support.
TM/Ps appear to function best when they are adaptable scaffolds that support, rather than replace, clinical judgement, relational work, and musical spontaneity.

For TM/Ps to be widely adopted, they will likely need to offer clear benefits (e.g. for interdisciplinary communication or documentation) while explicitly allowing room for improvisation, client preference, and therapist-led adaptation (Flückiger et al., 2018).

text.text: This study has several limitations.
First, the sample size was relatively modest (N = 93) and recruited via online networks, which may have introduced self-selection bias.

It is unclear whether the sample appears skewed towards therapists who rarely or only occasionally use TM/Ps, or whether it actually represents the general population of therapists or not, which would limit the generalisability of the findings and may amplify particular views on standardisation and flexibility.

Future studies should aim for larger and more diverse samples, perhaps specifically targeting therapists who regularly work with manualised interventions across different regions and professional settings.
Furthermore, although the survey was translated into five languages, most of the responses were in Dutch and English, with only a few responses in German, Greek, and Spanish.
This imbalance precluded formal comparisons between language groups and may have obscured potential cultural or contextual differences in TM/P use and attitudes.
Third, the survey instrument was newly developed and, although content-validated by experienced therapists and native speakers, it has not undergone formal psychometric validation.
Some items could be construed as double-barrelled (combining closely related concepts, such as spontaneity P r e p r i n t

and play), several attitude items are negatively framed, and the list of reasons for deviating from or not using TM/Ps was pre-composed by the authors.

These design choices reflect concerns commonly reported in practice and our intention to include both positive and negative statements as a method to reduce response biases, but they may also constrain responses and reflect our own assumptions and biases about TM/Ps.
We consider these issues important to add refinement in future survey development.

Finally, an important limitation on interpreting the statistical outcomes is that the results were not corrected for multiple tests, and as the effects were modest in size, they would not have survived this correction.
The choice to do this was based on the exploratory nature of the investigation, deeming it useful even with this caveat to report the patterns found in the data.
However, it does mean these results should be interpreted cautiously, and replication in larger samples is needed.
As such, while these findings should be interpreted as preliminary and hypothesis-generating, rather than confirmatory, we believe that they will be valuable to future, adequately powered studies.

Future research could integrate qualitative methods to examine in more depth how therapists across different approaches and settings understand TM/Ps, how they make decisions to adhere or deviate in specific clinical situations, and how they negotiate motivation when working with more or less structured interventions.
Mixed-methods designs could also help clarify how therapist attitudes, contextual factors, and specific features of TM/Ps interact to shape both motivation and clinical outcomes.
In this sample, music therapists tended to prioritise individualised work over strict adherence to TM/Ps, often modifying protocols to maintain musical spontaneity and engagement.
At the same time, respondents noted that having some structure can support consistency and collaboration with other professionals when it is applied flexibly rather than rigidly.

Overall, the findings suggest that TM/Ps are most helpful when they offer direction without overly narrowing therapists' choices in how they work with clients or attend to both client and therapist motivation.
